Food Services and its Impact on Wellbeing Indicators
Authored by: Katrine Chan
Date Created: 2024
Time to Complete: 90 mins
Level: Intermediate
Prerequisite Skills: Python
Scenario
As a community planner at the City of Melbourne, I want to understand the availability of food support services and how they relate to wellbeing indicators across the community, so that I can identify gaps in service provision and make informed decisions that strengthen food security and improve overall community wellbeing.
What this usecase will teach you
By working through this notebook, you will learn how to fetch and combine two real open datasets, explore wellbeing and support service data, and build a simple forecasting model to understand trends in food security.
  • How to fetch datasets from the Melbourne Open Data Portal using a REST API
  • How to identify and handle missing values in real world survey data
  • How to visualise service availability using bar charts, a word cloud, and an interactive map
  • How to filter a broader dataset down to a specific topic of interest, such as food security
  • How to fit a simple time series model and interpret its forecast, including its limitations
Background
The City of Melbourne recognises that access to support services plays an important role in personal wellbeing and social connection. Food support is a basic necessity, and reliable access to food affects physical health, mental wellbeing, and a sense of security. Understanding how food services are distributed across the city, and how this relates to wellbeing indicators, helps the council identify where support may be lacking and where food security could be strengthened. This is important for preventing food insecurity, which can lead to poor health, social isolation, and increased stress.
Data Sets
This analysis combines two Melbourne Open Data Portal datasets:
  • Indicators of Wellbeing by Year (Future Melbourne), accessed 26 August 2026, an annual survey of personal wellbeing, social connection, and food security among Melbourne residents, covering 2012 to 2016
  • Free and Cheap Support Services, with Opening Hours, Public Transport and Parking, accessed 26 August 2026, a list of free and low cost support services in Melbourne, including food, accommodation, health, and legal services

  2. Fetching the Wellbeing Indicators Dataset
  3. Understanding and Preparing the Wellbeing Indicators Data

  8. Focusing on Food Security Indicators

        8.2. Forecasting Food Security Trends with ARIMA
  9. Conclusion

base_url = 'https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/'
# apikey = ''

format = 'csv'

url = f'{base_url}{dataset_id}/exports/{format}'
params = {
    'select': '*',
    'limit': -1, # all records
    'lang': 'en',
    'timezone': 'UTC'
    #'api_key': apikey
}

#GET request

if response.status_code == 200:
    # StringIO to read the CSV data
    url_content = response.content.decode('utf-8')
    fm_df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(url_content), delimiter= ';')
else: 
    print(f'Request failed with status code{response.status_code}')

4. Exploring Wellbeing Indicator Trends
The chart below lets you choose any wellbeing indicator from a dropdown menu and view its trend from 2012 to 2016. This dropdown is interactive and requires a live kernel to explore other options; a static chart for total food insecurity, the indicator this analysis focuses on, is also shown directly below it.
In [8]:
# Creating an interactive plot, so plot will update according to the indicator selected by the user from the dropdown

# Function to plot the observations
def plot_trend(indicator_label):
    
    # Pick up the row selected by the user
    selected_data = fm_df[fm_df['indicator_label'] == indicator_label] 
    
    if not selected_data.empty:  # Checking to ensure selected data is not empty
        years = ['2012', '2013', '2014', '2015', '2016']
        values = selected_data[years].values[0]
        
        # Plot is then created 
        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
        plt.plot(years, values, marker='o')
        plt.title(f'Trend for {indicator_label}')
        plt.xlabel('Year')
        plt.ylabel('Percentage')
        plt.grid(True)
        plt.show()
    else:
        print(f"No data available for {indicator_label}")

# Create the dropdown widget, allowing user to pick an indicator.  Options in the drop down are unique values from the indicator_label column 
indicator_dropdown = widgets.Dropdown(
    options=fm_df['indicator_label'].unique(),
    description='Indicator:')

# Use interact to create the interactive plot, linking a function and a widget
interact(plot_trend, indicator_label=indicator_dropdown)

# A static view of one indicator is shown directly below, so a chart is visible even
# when this notebook is viewed as a static export without a live kernel
plot_trend('Total Food insecurity')

6.1. Handling Missing Geocoded Locations
Entries without a geocoded location have limited information and cannot be plotted on a map, so most will be removed. However, some helpline services lack a geocode but are still important to keep, so their details are stored separately before they are removed from the data used for mapping.
In [15]:
# Filter the DataFrame to include only rows where category_1 is 'Helpful phone number'

# Function to create a map centered at a specific location
def create_map():
    return folium.Map(location=[-37.81534, 144.97215], zoom_start=13)  # Somewhere in Melbourne so the map is more centered

# Function to format opening hours
def format_hours(row):
    # Creating "hours" List - If value in each row is not NA then print out the value 
    hours = [ 
        f"Monday: {row['monday']}" if pd.notna(row['monday']) else "Monday: Time Not Available", 
        f"Tuesday: {row['tuesday']}" if pd.notna(row['tuesday']) else "Tuesday: Time Not Available",
        f"Wednesday: {row['wednesday']}" if pd.notna(row['wednesday']) else "Wednesday: Time Not Available",
        f"Thursday: {row['thursday']}" if pd.notna(row['thursday']) else "Thursday: Time Not Available",
        f"Friday: {row['friday']}" if pd.notna(row['friday']) else "Friday: Time Not Available",
        f"Saturday: {row['saturday']}" if pd.notna(row['saturday']) else "Saturday: Time Not Available",
        f"Sunday: {row['sunday']}" if pd.notna(row['sunday']) else "Sunday: Time Not Available",
        f"Public Holiday: {row['public_holidays']}" if pd.notna(row['public_holidays']) else "Public Holiday: Time Not Available"
    ]
    return "<br>".join(hours)

# Function to add markers to the map
def add_markers(data, map_obj):
    for index, row in data.iterrows():
        name = row['name']
        phone = row['phone']
        latitude = row['latitude']
        longitude = row['longitude']
        category = row['category_1']
        hours_info = format_hours(row)  # Get formatted opening hours
        tooltip_text = f'<b>Name: {name}</b><br><b>Phone: {phone}</b><br>{hours_info}'  # Display name, phone, and hours in the tooltip
        
        # Obtain category colour from category_colours
        color = category_colors.get(category)  
        
        # Create a custom HTML marker using DivIcon
        html = f'<div style="background-color: {color}; width: 12px; height: 12px; border-radius: 50%; display: flex;"> </div>'
        icon = folium.DivIcon(html=html)
        
        # Use folium.DivIcon to create colored markers
        folium.Marker(
            [latitude, longitude], # Coordinates for the marker
            tooltip=tooltip_text, # Tooltip
            icon=icon # custom icon from above
        ).add_to(map_obj)

8.2. Forecasting Food Security Trends with ARIMA
Having identified the key indicators related to food insecurity in the City of Melbourne, the yearly mean of these indicators is calculated to explore future trends. Understanding whether these indicators are increasing or decreasing helps inform whether food service assistance should be expanded or reduced in different parts of Melbourne.
In [26]:
# Working out Yearly mean
year_columns = ['2012', '2013', '2014', '2015', '2016']
average_per_year = fs[year_columns].mean()

print("Average values per year, in percentage:")
average_per_year

Average values per year, in percentage:
Out[26]:
2012    6.425
2013    5.290
2014    6.585
2015    5.525
2016    6.170
dtype: float64
ARIMA, short for AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average, is a common method for forecasting values in a time series, such as a yearly average measured over several years. It combines three simple ideas: using past values to predict future ones (the AR, or autoregressive, part), working with the differences between consecutive values to make the trend easier to model (the I, or integrated, part), and using past forecast errors to improve the next prediction (the MA, or moving average, part). Each of these three ideas has a setting, generally written as p, d, and q, and the best combination is not known in advance. A grid search is used below to try a range of combinations and keep the one that fits the data best.
This dataset only has five yearly data points, from 2012 to 2016. A model with several settings fitted to only five observations is at real risk of overfitting, meaning it may fit the historical values closely without actually capturing a genuine underlying trend. The forecast below should therefore be read as an exploratory estimate rather than a statistically robust prediction, and some of the parameter combinations tried in the grid search may fail to fit or produce unreliable results, which would not be unexpected given how little data is available.
In [27]:
# Using ARIMA with a grid search to find the best p, d, q combination to forecast food security for the next 10 years
import warnings as _warnings

# Prepare data
data = average_per_year
data.index = pd.date_range(start='2012', periods=len(data), freq='YE')

# Define parameter grid for ARIMA (p, d, q)
p = d = q = range(0, 3)
pdq = list(product(p, d, q))

# Grid Search for ARIMA Parameters
def grid_search_arima(data, pdq):
    best_aic = np.inf  # Initialising positive infinity
    best_pdq = None
    best_model = None
    n_converged = 0

    # Warnings from failed or unstable fits are expected with this little data,
    # so they are suppressed only for the duration of the model fitting below
    with _warnings.catch_warnings():
        _warnings.simplefilter('ignore')
        for param in pdq:
            try:
                model = ARIMA(data, order=param)
                results = model.fit()
                n_converged += 1
                aic = results.aic
                if aic < best_aic:
                    best_aic = aic
                    best_pdq = param
                    best_model = results
            except Exception:
                continue

    print(f"{n_converged} of {len(pdq)} parameter combinations converged.")
    return best_pdq, best_model

# Perform Grid Search and print
best_pdq, best_model = grid_search_arima(data, pdq)
print('Best ARIMA parameters:', best_pdq)

# Forecast the next 10 years using the best model
forecast_steps = 10
forecast = best_model.forecast(steps=forecast_steps)
forecast_index = pd.date_range(start=data.index[-1] + pd.DateOffset(years=1), periods=forecast_steps, freq='YE')

# Combine historical and forecasted data for plotting
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.plot(data.index, data, label='Historical Data', marker='o')
plt.plot(forecast_index, forecast, label='Forecast', color='red', marker='o')

# Plot formatting
plt.title('Food Insecurity Forecast for the 10 Years Following the Last Surveyed Year')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Average Value')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

27 of 27 parameter combinations converged.
Best ARIMA parameters: (2, 0, 0)
In [28]:
# Calculate evaluation metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE)
# Note: with only 5 data points in total, these metrics compare the model's fitted
# values against the same data it was trained on, rather than genuine held out data.
# They give a rough sense of in sample fit only, not a true measure of forecast accuracy.
actual_values = data.values[-5:]  # Last 5 years of actual values
predicted_values = best_model.fittedvalues[-5:]  # Fitted values from the ARIMA model over the same years

# Mean Absolute Error
mae = mean_absolute_error(actual_values, predicted_values)

# Mean Squared Error
mse = mean_squared_error(actual_values, predicted_values)

# Root Mean Squared Error
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)

# Print evaluation metrics
print("Model Evaluation Metrics (in-sample fit, not held-out validation):")
print(f"Mean Absolute Error (MAE): {mae:.2f}")
print(f"Mean Squared Error (MSE): {mse:.2f}")
print(f"Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): {rmse:.2f}")

Model Evaluation Metrics (in-sample fit, not held-out validation):
Mean Absolute Error (MAE): 0.17
Mean Squared Error (MSE): 0.06
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): 0.24
The error values above are relatively low, showing the model fits the five historical points closely. Because these figures come from the same small sample the model was trained on, they show that the model can reproduce the historical trend, not that it can reliably predict future years. The forecast should be treated as an exploratory estimate rather than a statistically validated prediction.
9. Conclusion
With only 17 food services currently available in Melbourne, and food insecurity projected to remain around 6 percent, there is a clear case for the City of Melbourne to consider expanding and strengthening food services across the city. Reliable access to food is not only a matter of convenience, it supports personal safety and security, reduces stress, and contributes to a more resilient community. Addressing these needs directly can make a meaningful difference to residents' wellbeing.
10. Limitations of this Analysis
The analysis and forecast presented here have several limitations. As noted in Section 8.2, the forecast is based on only five yearly data points, so it should be treated as an exploratory estimate rather than a statistically robust prediction. The model also does not account for broader economic factors, such as inflation, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, or other disruptions that affect people's purchasing power and access to food. These factors could meaningfully change how food security trends actually develop. Regardless of these limitations, it remains important for any city to have a robust system in place to ensure that residents' basic needs, including food, are consistently met.
